# Draft:George Stocking's Gunpowder Factory

George Stocking’s Gunpowder Factory was one of the earliest known gunpowder manufacturing sites in colonial Connecticut, operating in the mid-17th century. Located in Glastonbury, then part of the Wethersfield settlement, the factory played a critical role in supplying gunpowder to the Connecticut Colony during a period of frontier conflicts and military expansion.
History
George Stocking, an early settler and original proprietor of Hartford, was granted permission by the Connecticut General Court to build a powder mill along Roaring Brook in what is now South Glastonbury, around 1654–1656. The site was chosen for its water power and isolation, both of which were essential for the volatile process of gunpowder production.
The factory produced black powder using traditional ingredients: saltpeter (potassium nitrate), charcoal, and sulfur. These were ground and mixed using water-powered machinery, which Stocking constructed along the brook. Given the scarcity of gunpowder in New England at the time, this local production was considered strategically important.
Significance
Stocking’s operation is notable as one of the earliest gunpowder mills in colonial America, predating many of the larger powder works established during the Revolutionary War. It exemplifies the colonial push for industrial self-sufficiency in the face of British restrictions and the logistical challenges of frontier defense.
The mill was also among the first recorded industrial sites in what would become Glastonbury, contributing to the town’s early industrial character. Although the factory itself did not survive long-term, likely due to the inherent danger of explosions and limited production scale, it set a precedent for later industrial use of Roaring Brook, including mills and foundries in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Legacy
Today, the site of George Stocking’s powder mill lies within or near the Cotton Hollow Preserve, a natural area along Roaring Brook managed by the Town of Glastonbury. While no structures remain, the legacy of the factory is remembered as a part of the town’s early history of innovation and wartime resilience.
